INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
In December 2012, a man carrying a semiautomatic rifle, fitted with a large-capacity magazine, entered Sandy Hook Elementary School and in
approximately four minutes killed 20 first graders
and six educators. 2  Following the shooting, families
from the school waited hours in the reunification center for their loved ones to arrive.  Some remained until
the governor informed them no one else would be returning.  Among those mortally wounded were sevenyear-old Daniel Barden, six-year-old Dylan Hockley,
and Mary Sherlach, the school psychologist.  In the
days and weeks that followed, parents and community members comforted each other in their grief and
became resolute that they had to act to prevent such
a shooting from ever happening again.  Those efforts
led to the creation of Sandy Hook Promise (“SHP”), co-
1 Amicus certifies that no counsel for any party helped author this brief and no entity or person other than amicus and its
counsel made any monetary contribution toward this brief.
2 As a matter of practice, amicus does not use the phrases
“assault rifle” or “assault weapon” because they are often contested terms.  Though that is the language used in the challenged Connecticut statute, see C ONN. GEN. STAT. § 53-202a
(2026), amicus uses “semiautomatic rifle” in this brief to refer to
the weapons regulated in the challenged statute.  See Nat’l Ass’n
for Gun Rights v. Lamont , 153 F.4th 213, 222–26 (2d Cir. 2025)
(describing at length the types of weapons defined as “assault
weapon” in the Connecticut statute).  Amicus uses the phrase
“large capacity magazine” to be consistent with the language of
the statute, see CONN. GEN. STAT. § 53-202w(a)(1), (b), and the
Second Circuit’s decision, see Lamont, 153 F.4th at 226.

2
founded by Daniel’s father Mark Barden, Dylan’s
mother Nicole Hockley, and Mary’s husband William
Sherlach.  Nearly 14 years since its founding, Sandy
Hook Promise has grown into a national organization.
It has instituted campaigns and trainings in
schools to reduce the risk of school shootings, including the Start With Hello and No One Eats Alone campaigns to address social isolation and the Say
Something program, including the Say Something –
Anonymous Reporting System, which trains students
and educators to recognize the warning signs of peers
experiencing mental-health crises.  Though it has
grown substantially in size, its mission remains the
same: preventing school shootings.
This is amicus’s first friend-of-the-court brief.  It
writes to urge the Court to affirm the decisions below
and preserve the practical regulations that the people
of Connecticut passed to protect their children and educators from another mass school shooting.3
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
On a Friday morning in December 2012, a 20-yearold man entered Sandy Hook Elementary School in
Newtown, Connecticut, wielding a semiautomatic rifle ( i.e., a Bushmaster XM15-E2S).  He fired 154
3 In the light of amicus’s Connecticut-specific experience,
this brief focuses specifically on the Second Circuit’s decision.
But amicus’s arguments apply equally to the Seventh Circuit’s
decision and the underlying Cook County ordinance.

3
bullets in approximately four minutes, killing 20 first
graders and six adults.  That night, as families
grieved and waited to learn the names of the children
who had been killed, members of the community knew
they had to act.
After four months of advocacy by amicus and a
broad coalition of community members, the Connecticut Legislature strengthened its existing law to ban
possession of the weapon and magazine type that the
shooter used, and weapons like it.  About a decade
later, the Legislature acted again to close a loophole
that existed in the law.
Petitioners now seek to overturn, inter alia, that
law and prevent any community from regulating
these weapons.  This case centers on the authority of
the citizens of a State to identify a grave risk to the
safety and welfare of children and to respond with a
narrowly tailored law regulating the possession of
certain semiautomatic firearms and large-capacity
magazines.
Certain semiautomatic weapons and large-capacity magazines are uniquely capable of causing masscasualty shooting events because of their ability to
fire a high volume of rounds in a short period.  The
Sandy Hook shooting, like many active-shooter incidents, lasted no more than five minutes.4  The shooter
4 Active Shooter Study: Quick Reference Guide , FBI,
https://perma.cc/M2WV-CN38 (last visited Oct. 27, 2026).

4
was able to fire 154 rounds in that short period solely
because of the semiautomatic nature of his weapon
and the large capacity of the magazine.
The effects of these weapons on children’s bodies
are catastrophic and obscene.  Seven-year-old Daniel
Barden was shot in the head.  Six-year-old Dylan
Hockley was shot five times, his body destroyed so
completely, his mother was told not to touch him to
say goodbye as he lay in his coffin.
Connecticut’s legislative reform also had to address the fact that the shooter possessed a lawfully
purchased weapon (as is common in many massshooting incidents).  So, the people of Connecticut had
to address a public-safety problem posed by assailants
who abuse their possession of a lawfully purchased
firearm capable of firing a high volume of rounds
without violating the Second Amendment.
The result is a law that has helped prevent a masscasualty school shooting from happening in Connecticut in the nearly 14 years since the shooting at Sandy
Hook.  Consistent with this Nation’s tradition of firearm regulation, the law removes access to the most
dangerous weapons and leaves available more than a
thousand alternative firearms for lawful possession
and use, including hunting, sport shooting, and selfdefense.  Petitioners have not pointed to any historical tradition that suggests otherwise.
The Second Circuit correctly applied New York
State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1

5
(2022), in concluding that States have long had the
right to address the risks posed by dangerous weapons through regulation.  See Nat’l Ass’n for Gun
Rights v. Lamont , 153 F.4th 213, 235–47 (2d Cir.
2025); infra Part I.B.
Petitioners seek to overturn that decision and disrupt the thoughtful and extensively debated firearm
law that the people of Connecticut have formulated
over decades.  And the path they ask this Court to
take in doing so is far-reaching.  They ask this Court
to break new ground and hold that if a firearm is in
“common use”—a term even they concede is undefined
and amorphous—then the people may never ban possession of the weapon.
This Court’s precedent holds no such thing.  And
how could it?  In Petitioners’ telling, so long as a judge
determines that a firearm is in “common use,” the
people forfeit their right to ban possession of the
weapon and the State forfeits its right to protect the
welfare of its citizens by regulating the firearm.  Parents, too, forfeit their liberty interest in providing for
the welfare of their children because they are left
without democratic recourse against the risks posed
by the weapon.  In other words, Petitioners seek an
immunity for the Second Amendment that virtually
no other constitutional right enjoys.
This Court has held that the Second Amendment
right is not unlimited.  In response to an unthinkable
tragedy, and determined to prevent that tragedy from

6
ever repeating itself, the people of Connecticut regulated an unusually dangerous weapon— i.e., a select
category of firearms and large-capacity magazines—
without violating the Second Amendment right of
their neighbors.
The Second Circuit’s judgment should be affirmed.
ARGUMENT
I. MASS SCHOOL SHOOTINGS ARE AN UN-
PRECEDENTED SOCIETAL CONCERN
THAT THE STATE MUST BE ABLE TO AD-
DRESS THROUGH LEGISLATION.
As the Connecticut Respondents and the Second
Circuit highlight, certain semiautomatic weapons
have enabled lone shooters to perpetrate unthinkable
and unprecedented mass-shooting events.  Resp.Br. 5
at 30–31, 36;  see Lamont, 153 F.4th at 236–40.  Amicus focuses on the narrower and deadlier problem
that precipitated the challenged Connecticut statute:
mass school shootings at K-12 institutions.
The Connecticut law at issue was a direct, democratic byproduct of the Sandy Hook school shooting in
2012.  As discussed below, mass school shootings are
a modern societal problem.  Lamont, 153 F.4th at
236–40.  The citizens of many States, including Connecticut, have identified that threat and addressed
it—not through a sweeping judicial decision—but
through the labor-intensive and deliberate legislative
process.  And citizens’ ability to protect themselves
5 Citations to “Resp.Br.” refer to the Connecticut Respondents’ brief.

7
from unreasonably dangerous weapons through reasonable and narrow legislation is entirely consistent
with the long-held tradition of regulating firearms in
our Nation.
A. The Unprecedented Problem of Mass
School Shootings.
School shootings were virtually nonexistent until
the turn of the century.  In the quarter-century since
the shooting at Columbine High School in 1999, which
was the deadliest school shooting at the time, more
than 398,000 students have experienced gun violence
at school. 6  Since Columbine, there have been more
than 435 school shootings.7
And the statistics on mass school shootings are
even more bleak.  In the nearly 14 years since the
shooting at Sandy Hook, there have been at least six
mass school shootings by a shooter wielding certain
semiautomatic rifles.8  Schools are uniquely exposed
6 John Woodrow Cox et al., More Than 398,000 Students
Have Experienced Gun Violence at School Since Columbine ,
WASH. POST (Sept. 11, 2025), https://perma.cc/6LCW-FNF9.
7 Id.
8 Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School (Parkland, Fla.):
17 killed and 17 wounded; Robb Elementary School (Uvalde,
Tex.): 21 killed and 18 wounded; Central Visual and Performing
Arts High School (St. Louis, Mo.): 2 killed and 7 wounded; The
Covenant School (Nashville, Tenn.): 6 killed and 2 wounded;
Apalachee High School (Winder, Ga.): 4 killed and 9 wounded;
Annunciation Catholic School (Minneapolis, Minn.): 2 killed and
30 wounded.  K-12 School Homicides , V IOLENCE PREVENTION
PROJECT, https://perma.cc/JWJ7-4R79 (last visited Oct. 27,
2026).  Though there is no settled definition on the number of
casualties that would constitute a mass shooting, SHP defines it

8
to the danger from these weapons.  Students are gathered in classrooms at regularly scheduled times, they
vastly outnumber the adults who could lead them to
safety, and they have little to no ability to defend
themselves.  These problems are exacerbated when
these shootings occur at elementary or middle
schools.  Those six shootings have killed 52 people and
wounded 83.9
That evidence confirms that these weapons are
unusually dangerous and pose unprecedented societal
concerns.  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27, 47–48.  This is the
societal condition the people of Connecticut legislated
against.
B. The People of Connecticut Legislate to
Prevent Another School Shooting.
Foreseeing the risks that fully automatic, semiautomatic, or burst-fire weapons posed, Connecticut
passed a law in 1993 banning possession of many of
those weapons.  See Lamont, 153 F.4th at 222; CONN.
GEN. STAT. § 53-202a.  Despite that law, on December
14, 2012, a person armed with a semiautomatic
weapon (which is now prohibited by the challenged
law) entered Sandy Hook Elementary School, fired
154 bullets in approximately four minutes, and killed
20 first graders and six educators.10
as a shooting with four or more casualties ( i.e., those killed or
injured, not including the shooter) for purposes of this brief.
9 Id.
10 Our History , SANDY HOOK PROMISE,
https://perma.cc/2XV8-RHR5 (last visited Oct. 27, 2026).

9
In response, a groundswell of citizens from all
backgrounds—including 24 people who had a family
member killed or wounded in the shooting—engaged
in the democratic process to pass a law that would
prevent another school shooting from happening. 11
Like most mass school shooters since Sandy Hook, supra note 8, the perpetrator of the shooting used lawfully purchased weapons when he initiated the
violence on December 14th.12 See Lamont, 153 F.4th
at 221.
So the people of Connecticut confronted a grave
threat to public safety and responded, consistent with
this Nation’s tradition, by regulating the purchase
and possession of these unusually dangerous weapons.  After four months of advocacy, debate, and drafting, the democratic process worked: Connecticut
amended its prior law to refine the restrictions on
semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines.
See Lamont, 153 F.4th at 222.  That tailored law was
prescient: it correctly anticipated that certain semiautomatic rifles would become the weapons of choice
for perpetrators of mass school shootings. 13  And the
law did not paint with a broad brush; it imposed a tailored restriction that left the purchase of over a thousand firearms untouched, including other
semiautomatic weapons.  See id.  at 249.  Nearly a
11 Id.
12 K-12 School Homicides , VIOLENCE PREVENTION PROJECT,
https://perma.cc/JWJ7-4R79 (last visited Oct. 27, 2026) (showing
that nearly all semiautomatic weapons used in a mass school
shooting since Sandy Hook were purchased legally).
13 See id.

10
decade later, Connecticut closed loopholes in the 2013
law, but as Petitioners concede, see Pet.Br. at 37, still
left more than a thousand weapons otherwise available for lawful purchase, see Lamont, 153 F.4th at 223,
225, 249.
That law is entirely “consistent with this Nation’s
historical tradition of firearm regulation.” 14 Bruen,
597 U.S. at 17.  Connecticut regulated both (1) an unprecedented, modern societal concern and (2) a dramatic technological change in weaponry, which
“require[s] a more nuanced approach” to identifying a
historical analogue.  Id. at 27; see Resp.Br. at 36.  And
the historical analogue does not require a foundingera statute addressing mass school shootings.  The
Second Amendment is not “a law trapped in amber,”
and a modern regulation need only be “relevantly similar” to the historical tradition, not a “dead ringer” or
a “historical twin.”  United States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S.
680, 691–92 (2024).
The Second Circuit upheld Connecticut’s law because it regulates “unusually dangerous” weapons—
the modern heirs of the dirk, the Bowie knife, and the
machine gun—arms a legislature may restrict when
used to kill or terrorize.  Lamont, 153 F.4th at 233–
34, 243–45, 249.  Legislatures have long been able to
regulate weapons “to preserve the public peace, and
[to] protect [its] citizens from the terror which a
14 Because the Second Circuit assumed without deciding that
the regulated firearms and magazines are “arms” under the Second Amendment, and proceeded to Bruen’s second step, amicus
will not address the merits of that issue.  See Lamont, 153 F.4th
at 235.

11
wanton and unusual exhibition of arms might produce.”15 Aymette v. State , 21 Tenn. 154, 155 (1840);
e.g., Resp.Br. at 9–23 (detailing the long-held tradition of regulating unusually dangerous weapons).  For
well over a century and a half, courts have recognized
that the legislature has “the authority to adopt such
regulations of police, as may be dictated by the safety
of the people and the advancement of public morals.”
State v. Reid, 1 Ala. 612, 616 (1840) (emphasis added).
That includes laws “intended merely to promote personal security, and to put down lawless aggression
and violence.”  Id. at 617.  And courts have recognized
too that laws which “exert an unhappy influence upon
the moral feelings of the [bearer]” of the weapon “do[]
not come in collision with the constitution.”  Id.  Privileging the Second Amendment right—as Petitioners
seek to do here, see infra Part II.B—over all other constitutional rights, and preventing the legislature from
regulating a weapon the people have determined to be
too dangerous “would be to pervert a great political
right to the worst of purposes.”  Aymette, 21 Tenn. at
159.
The people of Connecticut have acted consistently
with that tradition.  To curtail the grave threat to
public safety caused by an unusually dangerous
weapon, they regulated possession of the weapon.
And in doing so, they correctly anticipated what the
15 Amicus agrees with the Second Circuit’s historical reading
of “unusually dangerous,” Lamont, 153 F.4th at 233–34; id. at
250–52 (Nathan, J., concurring), with which Petitioners take issue, see Pet.Br. at 43–45.  But to avoid repeating arguments
raised by Respondents, see Resp.Br. at 23–33, amicus will not
address the merits of that argument.

12
rest of the country would come to learn: that certain
semiautomatic rifles would become the weapon of
choice for assailants who target schoolchildren.  See
supra Part I.A.
Petitioners cannot escape this clear historical tradition.  Though they acknowledge Bruen’s command
that “cases implicating unprecedented societal concerns or dramatic technological changes may require
a more nuanced approach,” Pet.Br. at 42; Bruen, 597
U.S. at 27, they suggest that this Court has held that
cases implicating the issue of mass shootings are neither.  In their view, Bruen and Heller both implicated
the issue of mass shootings, and the Court did not apply a nuanced historical approach there.  But neither
case implicated the issue of mass shootings.  Bruen
addressed a challenge to a regulation that required
showing a special need for self-defense to carry a
handgun publicly, and Heller addressed a challenge
to a regulation that required a license for at-home
possession of a handgun.  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 8–11;
District of Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 570, 574
(2008).  In deciding both cases, the Court never suggested that either regulation was enacted to prevent
mass shootings, particularly those targeting children
in their schools, and neither decision’s historical inquiry addressed the issue.  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27; Heller, 554 U.S. at 628.
At bottom, Connecticut’s law is consistent with
this Nation’s historical tradition of firearms regulation, whether under a nuanced approach or otherwise.
That historical tradition is inescapable here and Petitioners offer no persuasive answer to it.

13
II. PETITIONERS’ AHISTORICAL POSITION
IS UNWORKABLE AND WOULD PRIVILEGE
THE SECOND AMENDMENT OVER OTHER
RIGHTS.
Despite the Court’s admonition that, “like most
rights, the right secured by the Second Amendment is
not unlimited,” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 21 (cleaned up), Petitioners seek an unlimited right.  In their view, so
long as they can show a weapon is in common use, the
Constitution prohibits a ban on possession.  Pet.Br. at
24–25, 40, 49–50.  Their desired categorical immunity
confers on the Second Amendment exceptional
treatment, not equal treatment.
Given its background and interests in the resolution of the question presented to the Court, amicus focuses here on two arguments.  First, Petitioners
frame the common-use test as reflecting the will of the
people, but the test in fact immunizes the Second
Amendment from regulation by the people.  And they
frame the duly enacted law at issue here as tantamount to judge-made, empirical second-guessing.
That is counterfactual and an inversion of the parties’
posture.  Second, Petitioners’ desired immunity for
weapons that satisfy their amorphous “common use”
test runs roughshod over other constitutional rights.
There is no historical tradition for offering a constitutional right such exceptional treatment, especially not
at the clear and inexplicable cost of other constitutional rights.
A. Petitioners Seek a Common-Use Test That
Immunizes the Second Amendment from
Regulation.

14
Petitioners’ position in this case is that if a weapon
is in common use, its possession cannot be banned.
Pet.Br. at 1 (“ Heller stands for the proposition that
arms in common use cannot be banned.”); id. at 2
(“AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles cannot be
banned because they are in common use.”); id. at 40
(“Here, the relevant historical principle is that arms
that are in common use cannot be banned.”); id. at 49–
50 (“[T]he people of this Nation overwhelmingly
choose AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles for ordinary and lawful use and, therefore, a complete prohibition of their use is invalid” (citation
omitted)).  But Petitioners’ test, which functionally
seeks a common-use immunity, poses two fundamental problems.
The first problem is that this Court abandoned an
“intermediate scrutiny” analysis to inform the meaning of the Second Amendment in exchange for a historical analysis because the former analysis required
judges to “make difficult empirical judgments.”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 25.  To start, Petitioners’ commonuse test fails because it has no historical analogue.
But even if it could overcome that fatal flaw, the test
they invite this Court to adopt has not a single parameter on what is “common.”  Petitioners admit as much.
Pet.Br. at 24.  Judges would be left with the unworkable task of line-drawing around which weapons are
common and which are not.  Though Petitioners
would have commonality determine the outcome in
Second Amendment cases, they are unconcerned with
the “margins” of what that phrase means, see Pet.Br.
at 24, asking this Court to impose a new rule without
confronting the scope of the test beyond the most obvious examples.  In other words, they ask this Court

15
to impose a new rule that turns on a phrase they cannot define, which would leave district and appellate
courts in the lurch when resolving the flood of firearms challenges that would result from such a
groundbreaking new rule.  Cf. Resp.Br. at 48 (noting
that Petitioners and the federal government disagree
on how to measure “common use”).  The second problem is that Petitioners’ test would provide judges ample room to override duly enacted law—a clear
manifestation of the will of the people—if judges
thought the regulated weapon was too common.  Cf.
Pet.Br. at 39.
In an effort to preempt those problems, Petitioners
turn the dispute upside down: they argue that any
regulation of a weapon in common use overrides the
will of the people, even if the regulation was enacted
through the legislative process—the clearest political
manifestation of the people’s will.  Pet.Br. at 39.  Indeed, they argue that because the at-issue weapons
are common “it is impossible to conclude that the people have determined the arm is so dangerous it is unfit for use by ordinary citizens.”  Pet.Br. at 39.  But
the people of Connecticut did exactly that.  Aware
that the harms of mass school shootings they were
trying to prevent were caused by “ordinary citizens”—
i.e., lawful purchasers—they banned possession outright.  Petitioners offer not one word to address that
fact.
And that silence is made all the worse by how extreme Petitioners’ position is: in Petitioners’ view,
once a weapon has become common—a threshold for
which they offer no bounds—there is no political expression of the people restricting the possession of

16
that weapon that is constitutional.  Unsurprisingly,
Petitioners offer no historical analogue for such a position.
B. Petitioners’ Common-Use Test Would
Override the State’s Police Power and
Parents’ Rights.
If adopted, Petitioners’ test also would override
the State’s police power and parents’ fundamental
constitutional rights.  As described above, supra Part
II.A, Petitioners’ common-use test seeks a categorical
immunity no other constitutional right enjoys.  Their
test, which would expand the Second Amendment
into a limitless right whenever a judge finds that a
weapon is “common,” tramples other constitutional
rights, and violates this Court’s admonition that
“[l]ike most rights … the right secured by the Second
Amendment is not unlimited.”  Rahimi, 602 U.S. at
691 (quotation marks omitted); see Bruen, 597 U.S. at
24 (holding that the Court’s Second Amendment precedent “accords with how we protect other constitutional rights” which includes allowing the
Government to “prov[e] the constitutionality of its actions”); Heller, 554 U.S. at 595 (noting that the “individual right to keep and bear arms” is “not
unlimited”).
For example, under Petitioners’ test, once a judge
determines that a weapon is “in common use,” the
State forfeits its police power.  It forfeits that power
regardless of the level of criminal misuse associated
with the weapon.  Pet.Br. at 13 (“[C]riminal misuse is
irrelevant to whether an arm in common use is protected.”).  But “[a] State’s most basic responsibility is

17
to keep its people safe.”  Caetano v. Massachusetts ,
577 U.S. 411, 421 (2016) (Alito, J., concurring).  Petitioners’ test would strip a State of its inherent authority to police the use and possession of a weapon that
poses a significant risk to the welfare of its people.
U.S. CONST. amend. X; see United States v. Comstock,
560 U.S. 126, 148 (2010) (recognizing a State’s inherent police power).  And it would frustrate the State’s
use of that police power in keeping schools safe.
CONN. GEN. STAT. § 10-222n (2026) (mandating that
the Department of Emergency Services and Public
Protection “develop school security and safety plan
standards”); CONN. GEN. STAT. § 10-220f (2026) (permitting each local and regional board of education to
establish a school district safety committee “to increase staff and student awareness of safety and
health issues and to review the adequacy of emergency response procedures at each school”).
The result is that, contrary to this Nation’s history
and tradition of regulating firearms, the people of a
State are without recourse to regulate a firearm in the
face of “the terror which a wanton and unusual exhibition of arms might produce.”  Aymette, 21 Tenn. at
159.  Petitioners would use the “arms guarantee” of
the Second Amendment to remove from “the Legislature the authority to adopt such regulations of police,
as may be dictated by the safety of the people.”  Reid,
1 Ala. at 616.
By restricting the State’s police power to regulate
weapons which the people have decisively agreed
need to be regulated, Petitioners’ test privileges the
Second Amendment in another way: it prioritizes the
Second Amendment—which is a right available to

18
adults only—over the welfare of children.  Embedded
in a State’s general police power is a unique obligation
to the welfare of children, its most vulnerable citizens
who are unable to defend or advocate for themselves.
This obligation is enshrined in the Constitution’s Preamble: “We the People of the United States, in Order
to form a more perfect Union … promote the general
Welfare, and secure the Blessings of Liberty to ourselves and our Posterity[.]”  U.S. CONST. pmbl. (emphasis added).  And this Court has long recognized
“the state as parens patriae.”  Prince v. Massachusetts, 321 U.S. 158, 166 (1944).
To fulfill that obligation, the State regularly enacts laws that protect the welfare of children.  E.g.,
CONN. GEN. STAT. § 14-100a(d)(1)(C) (2026) (state law
mandating various “child restraint system[s]” or
booster seats for children traveling in motor vehicles
based on their age and weight); C ONN. GEN. STAT.
§ 53-21 (2026) (state law penalizing “[a]ny person who
… willfully or unlawfully causes or permits any child
under the age of sixteen years to be placed in such a

or does any act likely to impair the health or morals
of any such child[.]”); C ONN. BLDG. CODE, R326.6,
R326.6.1 (2018) (requiring a four-foot fence around
residential outdoor swimming pools to prevent drownings).  Petitioners’ test would hamstring the State
from fulfilling that obligation.
Another liberty interest would be overridden too:
the liberty “interest of parents in the care, custody,
and control of their children.”  Troxel v. Granville, 530

has described that right as “perhaps the oldest of the
fundamental liberty interests recognized by this

host of measures to keep their children safe at school,
ranging from purchasing bulletproof backpacks to

CONCLUSION
Across three decades, the people of Connecticut
regulated the challenged weapons to, among other
things, protect schoolchildren from another mass
school shooting.  That law was tailored, leaving more
than a thousand alternative weapons available for
lawful individual use that pose far less of a threat in
the hands of a potential assailant who would abuse
his possession of a lawfully purchased weapon to commit a mass school shooting.  That manner of regulation—the purest form of democratic response to a
